articles.title: A Greece for all seasons: my autumn roadtrip through the Peloponnese
articles.summary: An out-of-season journey through the peninsula reveals Byzantine villages, deserted beaches and friendly tavernas. As I drove across the causeway which links the tiny fortress island of Monemvasia to the south-eastern coast of the Peloponnese, the Aegean sparkling on all sides, I recalled a line by…
body: The excuse for my trip to the Peloponnese’s deep south – Messinia, the Mani, and Laconia – fell between those two ideas. My mother has roots in the Peloponnese – a sort-of homecoming that I’ve long wanted to explore – and with the summer over and greedy for an adventure to myself, I set out by car, leaving Kalamata, the leafy port city and gateway to the area, on a coastal road circuit.

The two-hour drive to Monemvasia began with the Taygetus pass, winding through villages and cliffside tunnels as golden eagles soared above the firs. On the far side of the Taygetus, the road opened to Mystras, an archaeological Byzantine site stacked up its hillside. I climbed to the Paleologian Palace and its chapels, then descended, hungry, to the village of Parori, where Taverna Ores was serving syglino, the local cured pork, and an okra stew. I practised my flimsy Greek with the waitress and her mother, who kept one eye on a television gameshow while stirring the stew pots.
points: An out-of-season journey through the peninsula reveals Byzantine villages, deserted beaches and friendly tavernas.

articles.title: Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad)
articles.summary: From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power. Introduction by Luke Kennard.
body: I have an image of myself in 2011, pushing my newborn son in a big red buggy because he would only nap when in motion. As I traversed the streets of suburban Birmingham, I felt observed, glanced at, commented on in a manner that ranged from pity to reproach to disproportionate admiration. Daft that it should be a remarkable sight, I thought, but there we go. Probably I’d have felt less self-conscious if I’d followed David Bowie’s example and – as in one of the images showcased here – worn what looks like a dress.

On depictions of men and women in art history, John Berger famously stated that “men act, women appear”. Men were portrayed demonstrating their physical power and readiness for action; to assert their dominance. Just turning that gaze around and using the lens to capture masculinity feels subversive, maybe even a little undermining.
points: From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power.

articles.title: Tim Dowling: a literary festival in Greece doesn’t inspire much hope – and sadly, nor do I
articles.summary: In between talks on geopolitical doom, one woman says I put her off journalism, while another thanks me for doing the same for her son. I’m at a literary festival in Greece, standing by some sort of colonnade, drink in hand, fulfilling my role as a non-luminary.
body: “Why are you just standing there?” my wife says, coming up behind me.

I’ve been to lots of literary festivals without my wife, where I spend a lot of time either in my hotel room or in a dark corner of the opening drinks thing. At some point I’m usually required to give a talk, and then I go home. I do not, at any point, give off any light.

But I’m not even doing a talk at this festival; I’m just here to play in the band. We did it last year and we’ve been asked back. But we aren’t playing until the penultimate evening, and in the meantime my schedule is full: swim, rehearse, attend talks outlining different forms of geopolitical doom, lunch, swim.
“There are people you know from last year,” my wife says. “You can’t stand behind a tree all night.”

articles.title: Women just want to work out in peace. Why all the thigh-rubbing lechery? | Emma Beddington
articles.summary: On Saturday Night Live last week, comedian Shane Gillis made a pathetic ‘joke’ about the clothes women wear to the gym. It was puerile – but also pernicious. I’ve spent the morning doing Shane Gillis’s work: checking out women in the gym.
body: Well, reporting for duty from the weight room, here’s the clothing tally: eight women in leggings and T-shirts; six in T-shirts and trackie bottoms; five in shorts and vest tops; one in a crop top and leggings. It’s not exactly the Folies Bergère – there’s not much, I would have thought, to cause Gillis to blush. But maybe I’m wrong – how undressed, exactly, constitutes whorish? Is a glimpse of a female forearm a distracting provocation? Should we pull up our socks to avoid inflaming male passions with our slutty ankles when we’re doing step-ups?

There’s a long, grim history of women trying to do physical activity in appropriate clothes and not being allowed, or feeling able to. We might not be sweating in floor-length dresses and corsets like early Olympian women, but bros are still complaining about girls doing squats in shorts in their eyeline, staring, propositioning and commenting (the #gymcreep hashtag is a veritable rogues’ gallery of them). Even Gillis’s language isn’t, unfortunately, exceptional: after his monologue, fitness writer Mikala Jamison shared a message on her Substack from a man she considered a friend, saying a gym had “whores everywhere”.

articles.title: In a Sprawling Theater Project, 34 Playwrights Make Drama From Democracy
articles.summary: “It feels like the very pillars of a healthy democracy are under attack,” says Lynn Nottage, one of 30-plus playwrights who have contributed new works to “Women+ on the Edge of Democracy.” “I’m in a moment in my life where every morning when I get up, I think about, ‘What have I done to protect…
body: Heidi Schreck was about to perform her play What the Constitution Means to Me on Broadway one night when her mother called. Apparently, the Tony-nominated work—which examines gender bias in the Constitution through the stories of women in Schreck’s family—had neglected an important figure from history: a hotel maid named Elsie Parrish.

By now, of course, it was a little late; the show had long been locked, and was indeed about to be filmed. But Parrish’s long fight for fairer wages stayed with Schreck—eventually forming the basis for a new play, Searching for Elsie Parrish, which will be published this month in Women+ on the Edge of Democracy.

An anthology of new plays by female-identifying writers, Women+ on the Edge of Democracy was commissioned by the Flynn—a center for performing arts in Burlington, Vermont—in partnership with the Susan Smith Blackburn Prize. It features pieces by playwrights from 30 states who were prompted with two questions: What is the current state of democracy in America? What can history, global context, or futurism offer us in this pivotal moment?

articles.title: Self-Care Gifts for Wellness-Focused Foodies (2026)
articles.summary: All the best gifts to help your friends enjoy little moments of calm all year long.
body: Shopping for the wellness-minded people in your life can be surprisingly intimidating. They already have their rituals, their favorite powders, and the matcha whisk they swear by. But the right gift can make those habits feel even more special. And during a season that leans heavily into indulgence and nonstop plans, a present that helps someone slow down and reset can go a long way.

Whether they unwind with a candlelit face mask, start every morning with a revitalizing smoothie, or simply enjoy sipping a sparkling beverage out of a pretty tinted coupe, your giftee will love these thoughtful, useful self-care gifts. Consider them little moments of calm that can become part of their wellness routine all year long.

As far as making matcha at home goes, it doesn’t get much better than Rocky’s. The newer brand, which founder Rocky Xu started in 2022, has that cool kid aesthetic from their apparel to their tea accessories. It’s perfect for the matcha lover in your life who wants to level up their morning ritual and do it in style.

articles.title: 5 Lady Jacket Outfits to Wear This Fall, According to the Street Style Set
articles.summary: From everyday denim to tailored trousers, discover five fresh ways to style fall’s must-have lady jacket—all inspired by the street style set.
body: Prim and proper? Not quite! This fall the classic lady jacket is getting a modern makeover, with purposefully shrunken silhouettes emerging as one of the season’s biggest outerwear trends. Naturally, the street style set quickly embraced the look, styling the traditionally feminine staple in fresh ways throughout fashion month.

We saw it more than once with denim. For example, Vogue ’s executive fashion director, Lisa Aiken, gave Kallmeyer’s gilded jacquard jacket a daytime spin with wide-leg blue jeans and black pumps. British Vogue ’s Chioma Nnadi, meanwhile, gave a pink lady jacket a maximalist feel by pairing it with a denim midiskirt and lace-up flats. Elsewhere on the streets of Paris, one off-duty model sported a classic black take with straight-leg blue jeans and, for an unexpected touch of luxury, elbow-length leather gloves.
But with jeans isn’t the only way to wear them. Below are five outfit ideas to make it your own, whether you’re heading into the office (hello, new power suits!) or out for drinks downtown.
points: From everyday denim to tailored trousers, discover five fresh ways to style fall’s must-have lady jacket—all inspired by the street style set.

articles.title: 20 Extraordinary Shops Worth Traveling For, Chosen by The Shopkeepers
articles.summary: From 100-year-old family-run operations to contemporary boutiques, these beautiful shops each offer a distinct sense of place and a dedication to craft.
body: When distinguishing a great shop from a good one, several qualities come to mind. Perhaps the storefront is as beautiful as it is historic, with perfectly-aged signage alluding to a storied past. Once inside, you may find a hawk-eyed curation of many goods or a passionate pursuit of a single good. And the shopkeeper, the glue to hold it all together, can bring an irreplaceable sense of place and reason to stay just a moment more—or both.

While shops can close or evolve, Flynn is confident their legacies will remain. "[The book] is a tribute, and I think they’re shops people can always look to to be inspired.” From a 237-year-old candle shop in Lisbon to a townhouse-turned-textiles-museum in Istanbul, explore 20 of the most beautiful shops in the world below, courtesy of Flynn.
